title: Toaster
synopsis: Your dumb startup makes one product: a smart toaster nobody asked for. You have eight months of runway, a co-founder who's lost the plot, and a pivot meeting on Monday.

nodes.text: Your co-founder Aman comes in twenty minutes late carrying a different toaster, smiling. 'I have a new idea,' he says. Your CFO Priya, also a friend, has her eyes closed in a long, suffering breath.

choices.text: Hear Aman out
Postpone Aman until after the pivot meeting

nodes.text: The new idea is, predictably, not a toaster. It is a 'smart cutting board.' You sit with this for three seconds. You realize the toaster is, at minimum, our toaster. The cutting board would, again, be nobody's.

choices.text: Push back firmly
Validate the impulse, then push back

nodes.text: Priya hands you the eight-month runway sheet. Three months in we have to either cut burn, raise, or sell. The toaster has, on the chart, three small green dots. The dots are, you suspect, you, Aman, and Priya's mom.

choices.text: Cut burn first
Plan a raise first

nodes.text: An actual customer, a woman in her sixties named Janine, calls in. She bought the toaster for her husband, who has memory issues. The toaster's reminder feature has, she says, kept him eating breakfast on the right schedule.

choices.text: Pivot the marketing toward elder care
Add Janine's story to the deck

nodes.text: Your lead engineer Sam is, you realize, our only hope. He has been quietly fixing the toaster's firmware in his off-hours. He has, in his desk drawer, a prototype of a screenless version that sells for half the price.

choices.text: Greenlight the cheap version
Promote Sam to CTO before anyone steals him

nodes.text: Walking into the VC office you decide, in the elevator, what story you are about to tell. Aman has a different story queued up. You have to align fast.

choices.text: Tell the elder-care story
Tell the tech story

nodes.text: Aman, after the meeting, breaks down in the conference room. He says he's been lying for months — to investors, to his wife, to you. He's not, he says, a CEO. He never was. He wants to be CTO.

choices.text: Accept the role swap immediately
Negotiate a slower transition

nodes.text: A surprise: a national magazine wants to profile Janine and the toaster. They will be at the office Thursday. You realize the story has, accidentally, gotten ahead of the strategy.

choices.text: Embrace the story
Delay the press for a tighter pivot

nodes.text: You let three people go. The way you do it matters. You write the references personally. You give two weeks of severance you can't afford. You realize this is the hardest thing you have done at this company so far.

choices.text: Tell the remaining team the truth about the runway
Hold the worst details until you have a plan

nodes.text: The profile is, mercifully, generous. The toaster sells out in seven days. The investors who passed last month start emailing again. Aman, somehow, gets a Wired feature out of being the 'humble CTO who saw the truth.'

choices.text: Raise the bridge round on momentum
Stay lean and grow off revenue

nodes.text: Sam's cheap prototype is ready for a pilot. You ship a small batch to fifty elder-care facilities at cost. The feedback is, against all expectation, immediate and positive.

choices.text: Productize for elder-care directly
Stay consumer; price up the cheap version

nodes.text: The Series A comes in. The lead investor is a woman who, herself, had a parent the toaster could have helped. The conversation in the conference room is, somehow, both about a SaaS multiple and her father.

choices.text: Accept her term sheet
Take a smaller round with terms you love

nodes.text: Three months pass. Revenue, slowly, climbs. You stop watching Twitter. You start sleeping. You realize, weirdly, that running a business at human scale is actually possible. It is just unfashionable.

choices.text: Commit to human-scale forever
Stay open to bigger if the right opportunity comes

nodes.text: Three years in. Forty employees. Revenue real. The toaster has a small but devoted following and a real elder-care line. You go to Janine's husband's funeral. She hugs you for a long time.

choices.text: Stay CEO for another decade
Hand off to a more operational CEO and become chair

nodes.text: A larger appliance company offers to buy you. The number is, professionally, life-changing. You have to decide what 'enough' is.

choices.text: Sell and use the money to build the next thing
Stay independent for the customers' sake

nodes.text: Aman, post-CTO, opens, of course, a bakery. The bread is fine. The bakery has, perfectly, a smart toaster on the counter. You and Priya laugh until you cry the first time you visit.

choices.text: Make the bakery your weekend office
Visit often but stay focused on the company

nodes.text: Janine sends a handwritten letter. It says, mostly, thank you. It says, in the middle of the second page, that she has started a small support group for caregivers and uses the toaster as the shared metaphor. You frame the letter.

choices.text: Fund the support group
Build a feature directly for caregivers based on her group

nodes.text: A quarterly board meeting that, for once, is boring in the good way. Revenue is up. Burn is sane. The lead investor asks, casually, what you want the next ten years to look like.

choices.text: Answer with a small ten-year plan
Answer with a big ten-year plan

nodes.text: You give an all-hands that is, for the first time, less a sales pitch than a thank-you. You read parts of Janine's letter aloud. Sam, the engineer, blinks twice and turns away. You realize most of the people in this room have been waiting for permission to care this openly about the work.

choices.text: Make the caregiver feature the next quarter's focus
Make small, kind operational changes first

nodes.text: Late at night you open the bottom drawer of your desk. The first toaster prototype is there, dented. You hold it. You decide the shape of the next chapter, in your hands, holding the thing that started it all.
nodes.sceneTitle: The Toaster Box, in a Drawer

choices.text: Stay small forever
Scale it for caregivers everywhere

nodes.text: You keep the company small. It stays profitable. You take real vacations. You hire kindly. You realize, late, that the toaster was never the point. The team was. The customers were. The company is, by every measure that matters, a success.

The company grows into a real elder-care platform. The toaster is, eventually, one of nine devices. You IPO. You retire at fifty. You sit in your garden with a toaster you built yourself and think, with surprising gentleness, of how far that one stupid idea took you.
